comments.author: arjie
comments.text: My daughter receives books through this program and I was curious how it was sustained at a $2.5/book wholesale cost. Interestingly, the coordinating body that selects books, facilitates distribution, and negotiates wholesale pricing is the Dolly Parton Imagination Library, but per-book funding is actually entirely through local charities and so on. This means that where charities are unable to act as partners, children will not receive books, but it also means that the program can operate by growing and shrinking as local support (including from state and local government grants) comes online and goes offline while keeping the overhead for local partners low. Dolly Parton came up with the initial local structure for her region in Tennessee and David Dotson of Dollywood scaled the operation using this decentralized model. Very impressive structure that makes this sustainable. Here’s the interview where he talks about it: https://www.endbookdeserts.com/dolly-parton-imagination-libr...

comments.text: In Tennessee hospitals a nurse, staff member, or authorized volunteer will swing by your room in the mother-baby unit and sign you up. Then you start receiving free books by mail each month until age 5. An amazing program by an amazing person!

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点: ドレリー・パートン・イマジネーション・ライブラリの持続可能な運営モデルについて。各書籍の単位コストは2.5ドルで、資金調達は各地の地方慈善団体や自治体助金に依存しているが、全国的な運営はドレリー・パートン自身が構築した地域ベースのネットワークとDavid Dotsonが拡弾した分散型モデルで成り立っている。

・賛否両論: このプログラムの運営方式をめぐり、双方の意見が出ている。一方では、地方自治体や慈善団体の参加状況によって子供たちが受益できるかが左右されるという非効率性や不平等が指摘されている。他方では、地方の支援が減れば縮小し、増えれば拡大できる柔軟性が叱られ、低コストで持続可能な構造として評価する声もある。

・注目コメント: 5歳になった子どもへの最後の本がドレリー・パートン逝去直後に届き、「I will always love you」と手紡しの手紙が添えられていたというコメントが感動を呼んだ。また、入院時に病院のスタッフが母子単位で登録するティーマねーびーさんの体験談も紹介され、地元医療機関との連携強化が奏効していることが強調されている。

・主な議論点  
Chromeのタブグループ機能がタブ管理の代替になっていることが挙げられ、Overgrownが必要とされる背景について議論が交わされた。視覚的にタブの年齢を判断できる点が評価されたが、植物の成長によってタブの内容が完全に隠れてしまう問題や、成長率の調整不可能さが指摰れた。  

・賛否両論  
肯定的な意見では、創造的な発想や「Overgrowth」というテーマからの発想転換が面白いとの声があり、Trelloのタスクの老化表示機能に対比された。否定的な意見では、機能自体がユースケースが限定されており、既存のタブ管理ツールで十分対応可能ではないかという見解も示された。  

・注目コメント  
「Originally, I was thinking about blocking users from closing their overgrown tabs until they slash all plants, but I thought it would be too annoying...」というコメントが注目を集め、この機能をオプションとして追加することを提案する意見が多数寄せられた。これにより、意図せず閉じてしまったタブの復元や、タブの整理促進が期待できるとしている。

stories.summary_ja:
## 主な議論点
コンテキストエンジニアリングにおける「ポイズニング」の定義について、コミュニティで賛否が分かれました。特に、FireRedタスクの例でウエイト内の情報がコンテキストに影響を与える現象について、これを「ポイズニング」と呼ぶべきかどうかが議論されました。

## 賛否両論
肯定的な意見では、長いコンテキストはモデルの性能を低下させることがあるため、コンテキスト管理の重要性が指摘されました。一方、否定的な意見では、ポイズニングとウエイトの問題は根本的に異なる現象であり、混同すべきではないという見解もありました。コンテキストの最適サイズについても、長すぎる場合と短すぎる場合の両方で問題が発生することに対する意見の分かれがみられました。

## 注目コメント
「コンテキスト管理で最も努力を注ぐべきは、モデルに出力を戻す情報源（つまりプロンプト）である」というコメントが注目されました。また、「誰かが『Claudeが弱体化した』と言ったら、最初に聞くべき質問は『コンテキストサイズはどれくらいか』」という実践的なアドバイスも興味深いです。提供されたプロバイダーのネイティブコンパクション機能のベンチマークについての研究請求も示唆されています。

comments.author: 1n3nt0r
comments.text: I took a course at a college in '79 using fortran on a mainframe (though I was just in middle school at the time). I can't say I understood all of the incantations required (IBM had JCL), but realized it was "magical" and wanted to be part of this tribe. I saved up to buy a VIC-20 (a 4K computer) and later a C64, writing games for both. Those were magical days I will look back to fondly. That sparkle has not left, though I sometimes miss the purity of near-bare-metal systems of yesteryear. Like some in my generation, I saw some of the early phases of computing, pre-internet, and am altogether grateful for it.

comments.author: chr15m
comments.text: Conan the Barbarian and Below the Root on our Apple IIe. Tiny worlds behind the glowing Orange CRT. How do I make something like this? My mum (lol) helped me figure out how to get keyboard input in BASIC. I made a little game where an O character chases your X character around the screen. Core game loop. Browsing pirate CGA games at the warung in Pondok Indah, well outside the jurisdiction of US law. Glorious rack upon rack of tiny worlds to explore. Death Track and Prince of Persia. More BASIC and that gorilla throwing bananas. Later on the Multiline BBS. Talking late into the night with tech weirdos twice my age. All manner of mind bending ideas. Newsgroups. Punks and skaters and cypherpunks. Predicting what was coming, seeing the future we expected unfolding. Downloading Commander Keen over FTP. WinSock and Netscape. My first homepage. Downloading Linux and getting it running. Configuring XFree86 modelines all night lol. Turbo Pascal and VAX VMS at uni. My first job coding. Hacking out web backends in gnarly ass Perl. No databases just blatting and slurping comma delimited text files lol. Getting paid to do the most exciting thing there was to do, all day. Magic.

comments.author: christophilus
comments.text: For me, it was the creative, puzzle-solving, game-like nature of it. Then I got my first job, and I had 100% autonomy, so a friend of mine and I got to solve real problems for real people in the real world. It was a rush. Making people’s lives better through software is still the biggest motivation for me.

comments.author: Krei-se
comments.text: I started programming on my schools CASIO Graphics Calculator. It was slow but allowed some text based games we then shared. No internet so did it all from trial and error. Then ... i wanted a 3D Cube rotating. At 15/16 this was a bit too much i guess i had no idea about rotation matrices back then and deemed myself a bit dense. Never got around doing 3D stuff at work, only databases all the time. I dabbled some with ThreeJS but i guess i was still haunted. BUT THEN. Geometric algebra! So smooth. If you like tables and had problems with stuff like cross products or quaternions, didnt like copy pasting rotation matrices, etc. YOU WILL LOVE geometric algebra! It's like you meet 2 tables on a FK and bam its a volume (highly simplified!!) Just my 2 cents. Don't write yourself off if you did not do 1337 demos in primary school on a tamagotchi.

comments.author: burnedbyhell
comments.text: I started on a Ti-83 and better yet could take other programs online and load them and then modify to my desire. When the teacher said show your work I wrote out the program I made to calculate the equation. They banned calculators altogether. Once there was a computer I traded sleep to stay on it. I worked professionally for almost 3 decades and it ultimately cost me my health and mental health. It was often my own insecurities and anxiety that led me up the ladder. I left the field and went to work for something I believe in and my tech skills are like wizardry to these folks. There is a lot of blue sky to explore for people in tech.

stories.title_en: A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis
stories.title_ja: 10歳のCNNが肝癌診断で最先端LLMを上回る

comments.author: snitty
comments.text: This is an example of why I'm a little stumped about why people are excited about Jev-style decision models. For any application at scale it'd be way more accurate to have a dedicated classifier using the right architecture (neural net, bayesian, etc.) LLMs drive the cost of making those models down to near zero. Just use the LLM to make a thing that's actually good at what you need it to do.

comments.author: tasuki
comments.text: > I compared to a 10-year old CNN and to my surprise found that this was superior. I'm surprised he's surprised. > A small, old, specialised network using an outdated architecture recognises skin lesions far better than two frontier LLMs. Yes of course. A 30m params Katago network with one playout is superhuman in playing go, while frontier LLMs have over 10,000 times more parameters and aren't any good at playing go. They're good at other things (such as helping you create a network that's good at playing go).

comments.author: Legend2440
comments.text: > I used Inception v3 pretrained on everyday photographs and then fine-tuned all layers on 68,011 dermoscopic and clinical images from the ISIC Archive on a single H100 GPU. >These 200 test lesions, and every other photograph of the same lesion or patient, were removed from its data (including the validation set) before training, so it had never seen them, and they were not used to choose the model or set its threshold. This is just benchmaxxing. A benchmaxxed model will always beat an unbenchmaxxed model, but it will be brittle. You can always beat a specific dataset with a small model by finetuning on a train/test split. But it doesn't generalize well to 'wild' images, because they are out-of-domain.

comments.author: MitPitt
comments.text: And a calculator outperforms LLMs at multiplication and division...

comments.author: jonex
comments.text: As people have mentioned, it isn't that surprising that a specially trained model beats a general purpose model. However, I think it kinda misses the potential of llms for diagnosis. What happens if we also include journal notes? What if we let the model generate questions to ask the patient and include those? What if the images aren't perfect examples and happen to contain out of distribution content like a tattoo?

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
本記事では、10年前のCNNモデルが最先端のLLM（大規模言語モデル）を上回る皮膚がん診断精度について議論が巻き起こした。コミュニティの間で最も多く言及されたのは、「特殊用途向けにチューニングされたモデル」と「汎用性の高いLLM」の性能比較であり、特にベンチマーク最適化（benchmaxing）されたモデルが特定データセットにおいて優位に立つことが自然な現象であるとして、モデル設計の方向性についての考察が展開された。

**賛否両諪**  
一方では、LLMの汎用性や推論能力を誇張しているとの批判もあり、「電卓でさえ掛け算や割り算でLLMを超える」との皮肉も出された。しかし、他のコメントからはLLMの臨床応用の可能性に言及する意見もあり、例えばジャーナルノートの統合、患者への質問生成、タトゥーのあるようなOutOfDistribution画像の処理など、様々な追加情報をLLMがどのように活用できるかについての期待が示された。

**注目コメント**  
「ベンチマーク最適化されたモデルは常に特定データセットで未最適化モデルを凌ぐが、野生の画像（out-of-domain）には脆弱になる」というコメントは、モデルの汎化能力に対する懸念を浮き彫りにした。また、「LLMは皮膺がん診断のようなタスクに特化したモデルを作るためのツールとして利用されるべき」という見解もあり、LLMの役割再定義が求えられている。

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
コメントでは、アメリカ各地でFOIA（Freedom of Information Act）請求に対して極端に高額な料金を請求する事例が問題視されている。オンジン州のユージーン警察の一件では、検索と処理に248万ドル、44816時間（約21年）かかると主張したが、これが非現実的であるとの批判が相次いだ。他にも防衛省が1500万時間、660万ドルを請請料とする事例も挙げられ、行政当局による情報開示拒否の新たな戦術として「料金設定による妨害」が指摰された。

**賛否両論**  
料金請求の妨害策に対しては、おおむね否定的な意見が多い。情報開示は市民の権利であり、請求금額は事実に見合わないべきだとの声が強い。一方、行費や人的コストを理由に実施不可能な請求をする行政庁に対する理解や、法制度の改正を通じた抑制策を求める見解も存在する。海外（ドイツ・英国）の事例も引用され、アメリカのFOIA運用の問題点が浮き彫りになった。

**注目コメント**  
「ドイツではFOIA相当の制度を巡り、政庌らの独裁的干渉が進んでいる」との指摩があり、彼らは高額請求料や個人のアクセス制限を正当化しようとしているとの批判が展開された。また、英国のように30日以内に回答を返す仕組みと比べ、アメリカの運善に対する「全く理解できない」との憤りが表明された。

comments.author: delichon
comments.text: Over the last four decades I've written several food logging apps for my own use. They've never been good enough to release, because I've always wanted more from them. But last week I made one in about a half hour that is by far the best I've ever written or used. I added a GrokBot, told it that it is my food logger, and to create a Google spreadsheet with the columns and sheets I need. After a couple of short iterations it was ready to go. Now to log anything I just prompt the bot with a little voice, text, or a photo of a meal, and it makes a (usually accurate) guess about what exactly I mean, looks up the nutrient stats, and logs it to the spreadsheet. To change any feature or refactor the spreadsheet I just describe the change and boom. Before LLMs this would have been magic for a sophisticated developer, now it's table stakes for the frontier AI vendors available to any muggle. This was Eunice slapping me in the face and shouting Wake Up!

comments.text: Man, I was about to go on a proper rant and claim that the site didn’t have every battle because it’s missing the battle of Maiden Castle… I claim no great historical authority here but, since I grew up mostly within sight of the hillfort, we were taught about its history at school to an extent that, at the time, felt unrelenting, cruelly repetitive, and utterly tedious. In reality though, it probably lasted for a single term at the fag end of 1985 when we learned about the Celts[0]. But what we learned was that General Vespasian captured Maiden Castle after a brutal one day battle in AD 43 in which Maiden Castle’s Celtic defenders were slaughtered in what amounted to a one-sided rout due to the superior weapons, tactics, and discipline of the Romans. This is what I remembered, but I wanted to look it up to ensure my facts were straight. Welp… TIL because subsequent investigation and analysis has shown that it didn’t happen at all so, no, dear reader, my “facts” were not straight. There never was any big battle. There might have been the odd smaller skirmish during the Roman period, but the bodies we found that were all supposed to have died in the big battle actually span several generations, dying at different times over a period of a couple of hundred years, and the evidence of violence in their deaths was in the vast majority of cases inter-tribal and occurred before the Romans even showed up. Maiden Castle had already fallen into decline by the time the Romans arrived and was mostly abandoned for a long period until a temple (that you can still visit the ruins of) was built early in the 4th century. So the reason the battle of Maiden Castle doesn’t appear on the site isn’t because the site is carelessly built AI-slop but because no such battle ever happened. I have been… disillusioned. Hats off to the human behind the AI that built the site. [0] I remember this with such precision because it was the first period of history we learned about at middle school, and matters didn’t improve significantly, because next it was the domestic matters of the bleeding Victorians, and lots of episodes of “How we used to live”.

stories.summary_ja:
このコメントスレッドでは、Hacker News 上の「Where the Romans Fought (interactive map)」に関する議論が underway です。 community の主な関心は、网站の可用性、歴史データの正確性、および生成方法に集中しています。

**主な議論点**  
社区で最も議論されたポイントは、网站のナビゲーションの問題と歴史的正確性です。特に、iOS モバイルでのナビゲーションが「不可能」と批判され、网站が AI 生成である可能性が指摘されています。また、ローマの戦いに関するデータの完全性が質問され、例えば「Maiden Castle の戦い」が欠落しているかどうかが議論の的になります。社区では、歴史記録の解釈や、学校で教わった事実の誤りについても議論が広がり、网站が実際の歴史研究を反映しているかが注目されています。

**賛否両論**  
意見が分かれている点は、网站の評価です。一部のユーザーは、ナビゲーションの悪さや AI 生成の可能性を批判し、「shitty AI website」と表現するなど、否定的な立場を崩していません。一方で、他のユーザーはデータの可視化や情報の正確性を称賛し、「very cool data and visualization」と评论するなど、肯定的な意見を表明しています。特に、Maiden Castle の例を通じて、网站が歴史的誤解を正した点が評価され、議論が分かれています。

**注目コメント**  
特に洞察のあるコメントとして、Maiden Castle に関する長文のコメントが挙げられます。このコメントでは、著者が学校で教わった「Maiden Castle の戦い」が実際には存在しない可能性があることを発見し、自身の記憶の誤りを反思。そして、网站がその誤りを正した点を称賛し、「Hats off to the human behind the AI」と评论しています。このコメントは、歴史記録の解釈の難しさと、データベースの信頼性について深く考察しており、社区全体の議論に影響を与えました。

comments.text: This statement stood out to me. > I have a similar thought about "there's no reason for software to be slow" BTW; in many cases, if you use AI to speed up some flow, you will add a bunch of messy code that will be overfit for the use case you tested on and will neither generalize, perf-wise, for all the use cases you should care about, nor will be maintainable upon future changes. LLMs have hardened hundreds of apps where I work. Maybe it's a language-specific thing. Most of the time, in Java, LLMs take into consideration tradeoffs (especially if they are part of the initial prompt) and actively explains them. It generally won't make messy workarounds, without a lot of extra prompting forcing it to do so. Ofc, if you have: - Functional tests - you'll be able to see it in the execution times of specific APIs - Stress testing - performance profiling is the most important output artifact

comments.author: fy20
comments.text: I think it's worth remembering that outside of our bubble the quality of software is pretty bad. I had a Hitachi heat pump (not recommended) installed earlier this year, and the software is pretty disappointing. It mostly works, but there are so many undocumented features and hard coded values that should be a configuration option but are not. For example when the heat pump reaches the target temperature it shuts off, then after 3 minutes switches on again. To prevent short cycling, I'd like to decrease the time between runs (so increase the 3 minutes) but that can't be changed. Somebody decided that 3 minutes is the correct value for everybody and that's it. I bought a €400 interface box (basically just a serial to IP interface, I guess $20 of hardware tops) to try and improve it. The €8000 heat pump doesn't come with WiFi or ethernet out of the box, you need to buy an accessory for that. It's not made by Hitachi, but it's an officially recommended accessory. One of what feature I wanted it for - which is advertised in their marketing materials - doesn't work. I emailed them, and they said it's probably because the display I have is a newer revision and doesn't allow access to the setting I need to turn on. And without turning that setting on I can't use the feature as advertised. They said I should email Hitachi and talk to them instead as it's not their part that's the issue. I look forward to the world where all software is either open source, or at least reverse engineerable to the point where you no longer have nonsense like this.

comments.author: 4ndrewl
comments.text: A faster postgres/regex is literally the faster horse metaphor. That software is a means to an end can be quite unfashionable on HN, but it's more ambitious thinking we need, and maybe software will be the answer. (and no, the wet dreams of a teenager's interplanetary conquest fetish is centuries old rehash, not original thinking)

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点
 community では、「ソフトウェアはより野心的であるべきだ」という原題の記事に対し、その「野心」とは何かという議論が中心となった。多くのコメントが、単なる性能向上（高速化）ではなく、ユーザーの本質的なニーズや、競争優位性を最大化する独自の価値の創造を「真の野心」として定義した。具体的には、既存の製品に新規機能を加えること（例：Kobo e-reader用アプリ）、または現在は不可能だが将来必要となるソフトウェアの構築が挙げられた。

・賛否両論
 議論の分かれ目は、AI（LLM）を活用した開発の位置づけだった。一部では、AIは特定の用途に最適化された「過学習」で保守性の低いコードを生むと批判された。他方で、適切な指示（プロンプト）とテスト・プロファイリングを組み合わせれば、AIは現実的なトレードオフを考慮した坚牢なコードを生成できるという反論もあった。これは、AIを「道具」として適切に制御する姿勢の重要性を浮き彫りにした。

・注目コメント
 特に洞察のあるコメントとして、非テクノロジー分野（例：Hitachiの熱泵）のソフトウェアが、設定項目の欠如やドキュメント不足など、極めて低品質であるという実例が挙げられた。このコメントは、 software が社会のあらゆる側面に浸透している現実を指摘し、 Tech community の「気泡」の外では、 STILL 野心的でないソフトウェアが多数存在するという現状を鋭く突いた。また、競争優位性を「faster ripgrep」のような改良ではなく、「只有あなたが指定できるもの」に見出すというコメントは、本質的なイノベーションの定義を提案していた。

comments.author: TacticalCoder
comments.text: Honestly that is just sad. Extremely sad. Bruce Schneier wrote about it more than two decades ago: "Unicode is too complex to ever be secure" . Systems created by people who have zero understanding of security and who cannot realize that complex systems cannot possibly ever be secure is already bad. But to then see the same people implement "security mechanisms" for the mess they created for in the first place is just sad. FWIW I love Unicode, where it belongs: in translation / properties files. I've got hooks verifying that all source code files are ASCII-only. I've got rules for my LLMs to only ever emit ASCII in source code. I've got firewall rules blocking any domain using punnycode (aka Unicode domain names). A bit tricky to do that one. I've got my editor configured so that any single non-visible ASCII char (except space and enter) and every single Unicode character appears in bold fluo magenta on a dark background. All zero-width chars are forced to have a width. I wonder how people who disagree with those who believe that Unicode is too complex to ever be secure reconcile with the fact that we have something titled: "Unicode® Technical Standard #39 Unicode Security Mechanisms" The question is: how the heck did we end up here? What mindset led to this clusterfuck? Who, in his right mind, decided that it was a good thing to have Unicode chars in URLs? Certainly not security experts. The homoglyph attacks were predicted by Bruce Schneier (and others) decades ago. Countless people got tricked and lost their live savings because URLs allow an 'a' to not be an 'a'. It's sad. And it's of course not the only attack using Unicode: there are plenty. It's really just all a sad joke and many of us saw it coming from day one.

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点
Unicodeの複雑さが根本的にセキュリティ脆弱性を招くという批判。特にドメイン名やURLでの同文字（homoglyph）攻撃の危険性が強調され、Bruce Schneierの過去の指摘を引用して、複雑なシステムはセキュリティを保ちえないという立場を明確にした。

・賛否両論
コメントは一貫してUnicodeのセキュリティリスクに否定的であるが、UTS #39のような標準が策定されている事実から、Unicodeの利便性を重視する立場と、セキュリティを最優先する立場の対立が浮き彫りされている。

・注目コメント
「Unicodeは翻訳/プロパティファイルに限って使用する」という実践的な回避策や、ソースコードをASCIIのみに制限する、ponycodeドメインをブロックするなどの具体的対策が紹介され、現実的なセキュリティ衛生の重要性を示している。

stories.title_en: AI use leads UC Berkeley math professor to see 'no point' in grading homework

comments.author: parsimo2010
comments.text: The irony here is perhaps missed by many. He didn’t grade homework in the first place. He paid assistants to grade. This is common practice among tenured professors with grant money to spend and graduate students beholden to them (I’m not making a moral statement, just noting this is common practice). Aside from the irony that Borcherds probably hasn’t graded a homework set in a while, instead let’s examine the purpose of homework. It helps you learn. You can read a chapter and think you understand the material, but doing homework makes you engage more with the material. Recently we’ve used the external motivator of course points to encourage this good habit. But this turns the relationship between teacher and student into a transaction- you do a problem, you get a point. And most young students really don’t care beyond that transaction. They are going to college to increase their earning potential, and that’s about it. So if we’re not going to rethink the purely transactional relationship schools have with most students, then you probably should stop giving points and grading homework. You have to figure out a new transactional structure that can’t have your tuition made irrelevant by a $20 subscription. That’s possible to figure out. A lot of people have pointed out various equity risks but it’s really just a matter of balancing the AI risk with the equity risk at the weighting acceptable to your institution. You could also attempt the much more challenging prospect of turning the transactional nature of college into some other relationship which fosters a student’s intrinsic motivation of learning for the sake of learning, but I bet your institution goes bankrupt in the process. So really you should just stop grading homework and put 100% of the grade weight into proctored assessments with some sort of firewall against AI tools. Anyone that faces an equity disadvantage because of this was probably also disadvantaged by the fact that you let rich kids with premium AI subscriptions get better grades on their homework.

comments.author: seanhunter
comments.text: As an aside, the professor in question is Richard Borcherds, fields medalist. He is probably most well known for proving the “Monstrous Moonshine” conjecture of Conway and Norton that there is some sort of correspondence between modular functions and representations of the Monster Group. When the conjecture was made in the 1970s, it was purely because someone noticed that a certain number was the same as the cardinality of the monster group. It seemed a crazy coincidence, so John H Conway said (playfully) that it was “Moonshine”. Hence the name “Monstrous Moonshine”. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monstrous_moonshine He has a youtube channel with lectures in number theory, category theory and other things.

comments.author: vhiremath4
comments.text: This is quite sad. Even if students would cheat off each other, someone had to do the homework. And even the collaboration of cheating on homework always served as a forcing function for me or others to think about the material. If not actively, at least in the form of a quasi background radiation. With AI that is completely gone, and without reward loops for incremental work, the truth is there is a large number of people (especially 18-20 year olds) who will not do well on the exams because they need a bit of a stick. I am not saying this as a black and white statement. I just think there are different cohorts of students based on maturity and self motivation and we might be losing out on one cohort that is at neither extreme.

comments.author: proc0
comments.text: With some exceptions I think higher education should probably go back to being about academia and not necessarily teaching skills for industry. I think companies can now easily invest in their own extended training and grab people out of high school. Just a thought.

comments.author: arjie
comments.text: What is the point of grading homework for college students anyway? The objective of exams is to determine mastery of the subject. It makes sense to have a grade act as a certificate of mastery. Grading homework is a measure of conscientiousness and perhaps a pedagogical tool to force learning but by college perhaps we should have moved out of the need for the latter. One can simply measure conscientiousness through attendance grade and mastery through exam grade and then we have two grades the universities can certify students for that are no longer dimension reduced into a single number.

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点
 community の議論の中心は、大学の宿題と試験の評価体系がAIの普及によって崩壊しているという根本的な問題です。多くのコメントが、宿題の本来の目的は「学習の定着を促進すること」であり、成績という「外部動機」に依存する現状が、学生の学びの本質を歪めていると指摘しています。特に、宿題に点数をつけるという取引関係が、学生の学習意欲を「試験で良い点を取る」という純粋な目標に還元していると批判されます。

・賛否両論
 議論は分かれています。一方で、宿題の採点をやめ、監視下的な試験に評価を集中させるべきという意見があります。これは、AIが宿題の取引を無効化する以上、評価体系を「真の理解度」を測れるものに変える必要があると主張します。他方で、宿題は「強制的な学習の強制力」として、自主性が乏しい学生層には不可欠だという反論があります。この立場は、試験だけでは測れない「継続的な努力」を促す役割が宿題にはあるとします。

・注目コメント
 特に洞察のあるコメントとして、 Richard Borcherds 教授の経歴（フィールズ賞受賞者）に言及し、彼が実際には助教に宿題を採点させていたという「皮肉」を指摘したコメントがあります。これは、採点の実態が「学習の促進」ではなく「管理の手段」だった可能性を示唆します。また、大学の役割を「職業技能培训」から「学術研究」に返すべきだという意見や、成績を「理解度（試験）」と「真面目さ（出席）」の二つに分離すべきだという提案は、評価体系の在り方について深く考察しています。

stories.summary_ja:
この記事に対するコメントでは、サムスンテレビの「ルートシェル」取得に関する議論が、調査方法の問題とテレビの監視機能の倫理的な側面に分かれて展開されている。

**主な議論点**
コミュニティで最も議論されたのは、調査者（OP）の方法論に対する批判である。複数のコメントが、この発見は「逆エンジニアリング（RE）」の基本手順を無視した結果であると指摘する。具体的には、公開ドキュメントやFCC申請書を読むという最初のステップを飛ばし、AI（Claude）に依存して調査したことが非難されている。その結果、サムスンが長年宣伝している犬や婴儿の検知機能を「新発見」したと誤解したとされる。

**賛否両論**
意见が分かれた点は、この監視機能の位置付けである。一方面、監視機能は製品の宣伝要素であり、ユーザーがそれを「機能」として選択しているという見方がある。他方で、テレビが監視機能を搭載すること自体に倫理的な懸念が表明され、「監視が機能化した」と批判する声がある。また、この監視がサムスンを訴訟のリスクに晒すかどうかについても議論が分かれている。

**注目コメント**
特に洞察のあるコメントとして、調査方法論を批判する最初のコメントが挙げられる。これは、REの基本を無視し、AIに導かれた調査者を「REの希望者たちの群れ」と皮肉り、その本質的な問題を突いている。さらに、監視機能を巡るサムスンの姿勢を「監視を機能として選択した」と批評し、HDMI入力をデフォルトでブロックする制限への不満を表明するコメントも注目される。これらは、技術的調査の適切なアプローチと、製造 manufacturers の責任に関する重要な指摘を行っている。

comments.author: xpct
comments.text: Ah, this prompted a few questions from me. Perhaps someone with more hardware background could chime in. They don't really show it here, but supposedly a Cerebras' chip is sub-divided into a 2D mesh of what they call PEs (cores). So data flow generally flows in two axis, and maintains consistent timings to its 4 neighboring cores. They show the layers flowing from left-to-right being streamed by PEs, but I wonder how true that ends up being: maybe the communications are easier to stream via diagonals, or some other shape that has better topology for data flow. Then, even from die shots of CPUs and GPUs we often see that cores are tiled as squares, and those don't have the same cross-core connection and streaming requirement. Now, I assume that some parts of what we call a core can be moved around more freely while maintaining whatever power/heating/timing requirements we have, so perhaps it's easier to 'force' a square by moving those loose parts around. But why do we confine those to squares? Is super-core layout just something not worth investing time into, like how interconnects are timed, non-convex tilings, and distances to I/O? And for streaming architectures like Cerebras, why aren't other types of tilings considered, something like a hexagon grid? This could have 3 inputs / 3 outputs, which could allow more complex data flow (?). Similarly, we could have 8 connections with longer diagonals in a square tiling, etc. I guess, what are the tradeoffs in place such that so many chip designs seem to reuse square tilings both locally and globally?

comments.author: cuttothechase
comments.text: The thing that is so confusing about this is the following fact - Lets say the frontier of some specific problem or a field in math is at x. X was reached over millenia by incremental steps and sometimes to leaps and jumps. Now if AI gives us a x + 1 or x + 10 state, aren't there still x + infinite steps to climb? Many of this the AI can never imagine and won't reach by itself without human assist. Yes, there is a temporary shock and awe because of all the low hanging x + 1 through x+ 1000 fruits for a given sub-domain/problem have been carpet bombed or whatever.. but isn't it turtles all the way!? Won't people soon find something more to develop and solve that takes it further than where it was of this infinite realm of exploration?

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点
AIが数学の進歩を駆動するツールとなりうるという楽観論と、 mathematician の役割や教育が根本的に变化するという現実的な不安が議論の中心となった。AIが既存の知識の「低の果実」を急速に収穫し、人間が気づけなかったconnectionsを発見することで科学全体に貢献できるという見方と、一方で、数学の研究方法やTrainingが大きくシフトする必要があるという懸念が対立した。

・賛否両論
AIは「John Henry」的な存在となり、 mathematician の生存競争を煽るという不安 versus、AIはあくまでツールであり、人間が解決すべき「hard problem」に集中できるようになるという希望的見通しが分かれた。また、IBMがDeep Blueの後Chess研究をやめた例に倣い、AI企業が抽象数学から撤退する可能性が指摘され、その影響についても議論が分かれた。

・注目コメント
「turtles all the way down」という無限の探索のたとえが特に注目された。AIが現在の前沿（x）から x+1000 までを急速に進んでも、背後にはstill x+∞ という無限の課題が残り、人間の創造性が不可欠であるという洞察が、AIへの過度な期待や恐怖を鎮める重要な視点として紹介された。
